articles.headline: A 'flying' Tesla Roadster sounds impossible, until you see what Lockheed Martin built decades ago
keyFacts: Tesla reintroduced the Roadster on October 15, claiming high-pressure compressed air thrusters allow the car to jump and flip.
Tesla stated that the full thruster setup is exclusive to the Rocket trim and is not approved for public road use.
Lockheed Martin previously developed a similar thruster-guided missile defense vehicle that was retired in 2009.
body: A 'flying' Tesla Roadster sounds impossible, until you see what Lockheed Martin built decades ago
Thrusters are as good at flipping cars as they are at hunting ballistic missiles.

Tesla's long-delayed and still unreleased Tesla Roadster was formally reintroduced on October 15 and besides an angular, Cybertruck-esque design and the ability to go 0-60 mph in less than a second, the company's big surprise was that it can fly. The car can't really "fly" in the tradition of Back to the Future Part II, but more through a collection of controlled falling, jumping and flipping maneuvers. While admittedly impressive, the concept isn't unique to Tesla. Experimental missile defense systems have featured similar uses of thrusters since at least the early 2000s, in a form factor that's now called a Multiple Kill Vehicle or MKV.

In the case of the Roadster, the supercar is able to pull off its much lauded kickflips thanks to two high-pressure air tanks and ten nozzles placed throughout the car that fire off compressed air to move and stabilize it. Tesla claims the Roadster can refill those tanks on its own, though the full thruster setup is also only fully available on the Rocket trim of the car. The Thruster trim only features thrusters on the back of the car, and the Performance trim doesn't have them at all. Importantly, Tesla also says that the thrusters "aren't approved for public road use."

Lockheed Martin's MKV project didn't begin in earnest until 2004, when the company won a $760 million contract from the US' Missile Defense Agency to build "the first system capable of destroying multiple ballistic missile threats and decoys with a single launch." That system carries several smaller vehicles that are designed to smash into missiles to destroy them, and it keeps itself aloft using thrusters that can quickly change its direction and orientation on the fly, not unlike the Roadster.

Finding actual footage of the MKV in action is tricky, particularly because the concept of a single missile system that can take out multiple other missiles has been kicking around since the Reagan-era Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), which is better known as the "Star Wars" program. The video below is allegedly of Lockheed Martin's MKV, but similar footage has also been associated with SDI — and Lockheed Martin didn't exist until 1995, so anything attributed to it before then is suspect. Regardless, that concept is what Lockheed Martin and another contractor, Raytheon, were working on in separate development tracks until the original MKV project was retired in 2009 as part of military budget cuts.

Besides their intended uses — transporting the ultra-rich and destroying intercontinental ballistic missiles — the Roadster and MKV have one other important difference: How their thrusters actually work. Tesla is pretty adamant that the Roadster uses cold-gas thrusters (specifically compressed air), which means they don't burn fuel to move what they're attached to around. Based on a 2008 Lockheed Martin press release, its MKV was used in "hot-fire tests" that suggest some part of the system burned fuel for propulsion. Considering no one currently owns either, it's hard to say what's better, but Tesla's is presumably less combustible.

body: Wu-Tang’s Once Upon A Time in Shaolin album has, for the most part, been extremely difficult to listen to, but you can now hear two snippets of the album thanks to the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out, which just published an episode all about the exclusive record.
We can finally hear some of Wu-Tang Clan’s Once Upon A Time in Shaolin album
Pablo Torre is playing the one-of-one album owned by Martin Shkreli, the feds, and now a crypto group called PleasrDAO.

Once Upon A Time in Shaolin has a long history, which Pablo Torre Finds Out goes into in detail. Disgraced pharmaceutical executive Martin Shkreli bought the only copy of the album, which cannot be commercially released until 2103, in 2015 at auction. Shkreli had to forfeit the album to the US government, and the government sold it in 2021 to the crypto art collective PleasrDAO, which has allowed it to be played at special exhibitions.

Pablo Torre Finds Out, working with PleasrDAO, hosted a listening party for the album where they played it for Wu-Tang Clan member Method Man, who had never heard it up until that point. The podcast recorded the event and Method Man’s reaction, and you can hear two snippets from the album at 32:30 and 39:02 during the show.
Method Man’s review? “I do not hate this album.”

articles.headline: All The Records GTA 6 Will Break, We Think
keyFacts: Grand Theft Auto 6 is scheduled for release on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick stated that the company has not disclosed raw preorder figures because technically no units have been sold yet and preorders can be canceled.
Research firm Sensor Tower estimated that GTA 6 preorders could reach 25 million by launch, generating about $2 billion in revenue.
body: After years of development and perhaps more hype than for any game, GTA 6 is set for release on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. Predicting that it will be an enormous success commercially is perhaps one of the safest bets anyone could make.
But just how big will the launch be? And what records could GTA 6 beat if it delivers?
Lucia and Jason in GTA 6.
The records

The last GTA game, 2013's GTA 5, was a huge hit right out of the gate. It brought in $800 million in revenue over its first 24 hours and $1 billion in its first three days . Even a decade later, the game remains a sales juggernaut, eclipsing 230 million copies sold and counting .

Rockstar's latest game, 2018's Red Dead Redemption II, launched with $725 million in revenue over its opening weekend . It's gone on to sell more than 87 million copies, making it one of the top five best-selling games ever .
Outside of Rockstar, Bethesda's 2015 RPG Fallout 4 had a gigantic launch, shipping 12 million copies for launch day alone , generating sales in excess of $750 million.
So to sum up, here are the records that GTA 6 is expected to surpass:
GTA 5: $800 million in 24 hours and $1 billion in three days
Red Dead Redemption II: $725 million over its first weekend
Fallout 4: $750 million on launch day

GTA 6 has enormous shoes to fill to match and surpass Rockstar's previous games and Fallout 4. But if Sensor Tower's data that projects 25 million preorders by launch is correct--or even close--then it should have no problem beating GTA 5's initial sales.

One thing working in GTA 6's favor when it comes to comparisons to past games is that GTA 6 has a higher selling price. The base game goes for $80, compared to the $60 that GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption II launched at years ago.

Of course, $60 in 2013 dollars equates to about $85 today when factoring in inflation. But even inflation-adjusted figures would likely show that GTA 6 has a bigger launch, if it becomes the hit everyone expects it to. And when Take-Two inevitably shares GTA 6 sales data, you can bet the company will present the data is the absolute best possible light, whatever language and specifics it takes to get there.
The numbers so far

Officially, neither Rockstar nor parent company Take-Two have shared any numbers at all about preorders or sales projections since preorders opened in June. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick said it would not be prudent to disclose preorder figures because they could be misleading. His argument was that, technically speaking, GTA 6 has not sold a single copy yet, as, in theory, every preordered copy of the game could be returned. That's silly, of course; it sounds more like Zelnick is staying true to his mantra of never declaring success before it occurs.
Whatever the case, Zelnick said GTA 6 preorders "vastly" surpassed international expectations, but he did not say what those expectations were or "whether they mean anything" anyway.
Zelnick said sharing real, raw data for GTA 6 preorders could mislead investors, so Take-Two is not going to do so.

“I’ve reminded people that we simply don’t know the demand curve because it’s just never happened before,” Zelnick said. “Given that, we think the raw numbers could potentially be misleading in a direction we wouldn’t feel good about.”

Speaking during Take-Two’s latest earnings call, Zelnick said of GTA 6’s preorder numbers, “No one’s ever seen anything like this before at Take-Two, or in the industry.” He added: “To be clear, we haven’t sold one unit yet. You can cancel a preorder.”
$2 billion by launch?

The research firm Sensor Tower has a "GTA 6 Sales Tracker" site that shows estimates for GTA 6 preorders, displaying 6.08 million through October 13, and that apparently includes any returned/refunded copies. The group estimates that this works out to $594 million in revenue so far, with a split of 74% for PlayStation 5 and 26% for Xbox Series X|S.
Sensor Tower's Karl Kontus said in an interview that reorders for GTA 6 could be in the area of 25 million when the game releases, which would amount to “unprecedented preorder performance.”

At 25 million, that would work out to about $2 billion in revenue, which would cover the game's development budget and the majority of the marketing spend, he said. Kontus went on to say that he expects the majority of GTA 6 preorders to come in the last week or so before launch, as the hype peaks. Currently, the preorder split is skewing toward the $100 edition, Sensor Tower said, but that makes sense since people who preorder early are probably more on the enthusiast side. At launch, Sensor Tower said it expects about a 50/50 split between the $80 and $100 editions for preorder numbers.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=klc0fQmAL6k
Launch is only the beginning

GTA 6 is being marketed as a single-player experience that will be available on console exclusively. That may be true for now, but everyone expects Rockstar to release the next evolution of GTA Online for GTA 6 , and eventually bring the game to PC. A recent report said the PC edition could launch sooner than expected.

The investment company Jeffries released a note recently that says Take-Two's stock is currently trading at a discount at about $200/share today, October 16, and could jump to $300/share. The company is bullish on Take-Two not just because GTA 6 is expected to be a huge hit, but also because the next version of GTA Online will represent another revenue vector, and the expected PC edition will create another selling cycle.
A scene from GTA 6.

These are not wild predictions. After all, GTA Online, to this day, continues to bring in steady revenue for Take-Two through its various microtransactions and the GTA+ subscription service. It's only reasonable to assume Rockstar would further flesh out GTA Online for GTA 6 and create even more ways for people to spend time (and money) in the world. As for the PC edition, it makes a lot of sense that it would drive people to pick up the game there if that's their preferred platform, and they could be double-dippers, further enriching Take-Two in the process.
A different console market

GTA 5 launched at the very tail end of the PS3 and Xbox 360 console lifecycles, which created a unique situation that no doubt increased the game's sales potential. Those consoles combined for an install base of more than 150 million units, so Rockstar had an enormous market to sell into. And as stated above, it sold fantastically in this environment.

Rockstar launched the game for those platforms, but then also brought it to PS4 and Xbox One, and then to PS5 and Xbox Series X|S in the years that followed, with new improvements along the way. People didn't need to pay again, as free upgrades were offered in some situations, but it can be safely assumed many people double-dipped.

GTA 6 is launching in a very different world for the console market, as the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S are today more expensive than ever due to tariffs, the AI-fueled demand for memory and components, the war in Iran, and various other global macroeconomic factors driving up prices. The PS5 has sold more than 95 million units, and it's estimated that Xbox Series X|S is about a third of that, so there are probably more than 120 million combined units out there.
What about the long run?

If GTA 6 does outperform GTA 5 at launch, that doesn't necessarily it will be able to catch up to GTA 5 over the long haul. GTA 5 has sold more than 230 million copies, and it benefitted from the unique setup mentioned above. The game also debuted prior to the live-service black hole that exists today, with games like Fortnite and Roblox sucking up time and money from the market.

While there has been talk of the PS6 and Project Helix family of devices from Xbox, reports have suggested those platforms could be delayed due to the complexities and headaches related to the current environment mentioned above. Whenever the next PlayStation and Xbox consoles are available, though, it's a safe bet we'll see GTA 6 ported to them at some point.

As for the massive market that is the Switch 2, GTA 6 has not been announced for Nintendo's platform. It may not be ruled out, however, as Rockstar reportedly conducted tests for this--but that's all they could be. Nintendo of America's president told fans to ask Rockstar about GTA 6 for Switch 2.

Another issue at play for GTA 6 is that console generations are much longer than before, due to the market factors described above. So while Rockstar was able to migrate GTA 5 to new platforms every couple of years, and reap the benefits, that could be a more challenging proposition going forward.

Despite these possible headwinds, I am betting that the next evolution of GTA Online is a bonafide juggernaut that will outshine the main game in the fullness of time. For one, I expect Rockstar to heavily lean into user-generated content and provide a generally bigger and deeper world for GTA Online that gives players more things to do and more reasons to stay. In turn, this could create more opportunities for Rockstar to monetize and create its own kind of metaverse. Here's to hoping Rockstar divulges the goods on GTA Online 2.0 soon.

GTA 6 is a must-have game for many people, but for those people on the fence who don't already own a console or want a new one, putting up $600 for a base PS5 or $500 for a Series S might lead to serious sticker shock .
Keep checking back with GameSpot for more on GTA 6 in the days and weeks ahead.

articles.headline: “thegentlemanpervert” producing AI CSAM is a NJ prosecutor, say cops
keyFacts: New Jersey Deputy Attorney General Brian Richard Fitzgerald was arrested on felony charges involving AI-generated child sexual abuse material, detectives said.
Officials accused Fitzgerald of using artificial intelligence to alter social media photos of real minors into sexualized images and distributing them.
Police said they tracked a Discord account to Fitzgerald's home and recovered AI prompts, scripts, and chats admitting to creating the images.
body: New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday.

In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests. After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.”
On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media.

Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address.

After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.”

articles.headline: Have a Meta business account? You’re consenting to AI scraping now, legal experts say
keyFacts: Meta's updated commercial terms allow web scrapers to crawl websites associated with business accounts, Nieman Lab reported.
News publishers are affected, and Nieman Lab reported Meta could avoid licensing deals for AI training data.
The changes take effect on October 30 without an opt-out, meaning publishers must accept web-scraping or leave the platform.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Meta Business Suite’s new terms allow web-crawling on publication sites, legal experts say.
- The change goes into effect on Oct. 30.
- Meta says the updated terms are a “consolidation” of pre-existing conditions.
Meta’s new commercial terms allow its web scrapers, bots, and agents to crawl websites “associated with” Meta business accounts, including news publishers, according to a report by Nieman Lab.

The terms apply to accounts that use Meta Business Suite’s account dashboard. Companies manage their Instagram profiles, Facebook pages, Messenger, and WhatsApp channels through Meta Business Suite. ZDNET uses Meta Business Suite to analyze and schedule posts across social media platforms.
More from ZDNET
What’s changing

The changes go into effect on Oct. 30, and Meta will not provide an opt-out, meaning publishers will either agree to the web-scraping or be booted from the platform. These are Meta’s new terms and conditions for web-crawling:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Publishers vs. AI companies

Meta could be avoiding entering licensing deals with many websites and news publications through this new web-scraping language, Nieman Lab reports. Tech companies need tons of data and information to train their AI models, but not just any data will do. Journalistic content makes for a high-quality dataset because it’s traditionally been fact-checked and edited, which personal blogs or other text scraped from the open internet may not be.

But, in part because of how AI search features have negatively impacted traffic to news sites (and therefore ad dollars), publishers (including Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company) have launched copyright lawsuits against AI companies for using their content, both for model training and providing answers to search queries without attribution. Several AI labs have forged licensing agreements with news publications to avoid this.
Meta defended its position, saying that it is consolidating its commercial and self-serve ad terms, according to the Verge. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.headline: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
keyFacts: The Australian government introduced legislation requiring social media platforms to allow users to turn off algorithmically recommended content.
Officials said the proposed bill aims to protect users from online harms, imposing potential fines of up to A$100 million for non-compliance.
Critics and the Trump administration argued the reforms threaten free speech, while major tech companies largely declined to comment.
body: - Published
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws â which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services â will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see â and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms â often unsolicited â serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s â a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scrollâ¦ that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services â social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more â to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features â for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women â and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (Â£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.
The challenges

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive â although a US jury recently ruled otherwise.
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' â like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' â and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.
Right-wing parties in Australia â and the Trump administration â have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake â they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 â after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds â is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms â though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

articles.headline: Oil surges to $110 per barrel for the first time since May
keyFacts: Brent crude oil surpassed $110 per barrel on Friday, reaching its highest level since May as wars threatened global energy supplies.
President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russia to reduce diesel costs, drawing condemnation from lawmakers in both political parties.
Friday's energy price increases will likely raise gasoline costs for United States consumers in the coming days.
body: A key oil price benchmark surged Friday to its highest level in five months, as investors assessed the impact of both the Iran and Ukraine-Russia wars on global energy supplies.
Brent crude oil, widely considered to be among the most important prices in global energy, surpassed $110 per barrel shortly after 2:30 p.m. ET, its highest level since May.

U.S. crude oil, which also steers gas prices, jumped 3.5% Friday to close at $101.41 per barrel. It was the first time West Texas Intermediate crude had crossed the $100 threshold, closely watched by both traders and the public, since September.
Friday’s price jumps will likely add to already elevated gasoline prices for U.S. consumers in coming days. As of Friday morning, regular gasoline averaged $4.32 per gallon nationwide.
Diesel futures also jumped by more than 1% Friday. The cost of this commercial fuel critical for farming and other industrial sectors has risen even faster than regular gasoline in recent months.
Stocks fell Friday, partly in response to the jump in energy prices. The S&P 500 fell more than 1% while the Nasdaq Composite sharply dropped 2% by midafternoon.
The price of fuel around the world began its steady rise this spring, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
But an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months has caused an even more dramatic price spike for diesel.

Russia has traditionally been one of the world’s largest diesel exporters. But attack by Ukrainian forces on its energy infrastructure has taken much of its refining capacity offline. Likewise, energy assets in Ukraine have been targeted by Russian strikes.
As a result of the strikes, buyers of Russian diesel have been forced to look elsewhere for their fuel supplies.

But there aren’t any clear opportunities to easily expand diesel production. Refineries in the U.S. and Europe are already running at nearly maximum capacity to churn out as much diesel fuel as possible.
President Donald Trump is intensely focused on the high cost of diesel fuel because of its key role in driving up inflation -- a top issue for American voters in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Trump has pressured U.S. allies to release some of their diesel and crude oil reserves, and he recently signed an order to ease regulations on the use of off-road “red dye” diesel.
When neither of these actions resulted in a significant step down for diesel prices, Trump made the decision this month to ease U.S. sanctions on Russia.
The goal was to allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to release some of Russia’s supplies to the global market.
But the sanctions relief stunned world leaders and drew quick condemnation from U.S. lawmakers in both parties.
While Trump has touted the deal with Putin as a way to lower prices, as of Friday, no actual Russian diesel had been identified as having reached the global market.

Russia’s refining infrastructure has been badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes. On Friday, another Russian refiner suspended some crude oil operations. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”
Additionally, a group of American lawmakers introduced a bill that would block Trump’s deal for Russian diesel. It has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House.

But polling indicates that Republicans are unlikely to maintain a majority in the House after November’s elections. The Russian diesel blocking bill offers a preview of the kind of legislation that could advance under Democratic control.
Yet even now, the legislation adds to “growing doubts that a U.S. — Russia diesel deal will come to fruition,” said Mason Mendez, global real assets analyst at Wells Fargo.
“Investors also remain concerned about further military escalation in the Middle East, as attacks on commercial shipping and regional infrastructure have increased in recent weeks,” he said.
“Looking into 2027, the need to rebuild depleted global inventories could create an additional source of demand and keep energy prices elevated for longer.”

articles.headline: Nonolith traps you in a living maze and challenges you to find hidden terrain magic using good old copy-paste
keyFacts: Nonolith is a 2D puzzle game created by Justcamh where players control a gnome trapped inside a living edifice.
Players can copy, paste, move, rotate, and delete chunks of scenery or activate hidden spells using tile patterns to escape.
A demo is currently available on Steam, and the full game is scheduled for release later this year.
body: After enjoying Echo Weaver last week, I'm in the market for games that gaze with utmost scorn upon the concept of unlockable abilities, smugly declaring that everything you need to complete them is available to you from the word go.

There was a time when the idea of a game without unlocks wasn't all that novel, you know. Indeed, you young people may be surprised to hear that videogames pre-date the act of unlocking. Genesis-era Sonic the Hedgehog never unlocked so much as a +5% SPD perk. Still, Genesis-era Sonic wasn't a bizarrely malleable 2D puzzler like Nonolith. Created by Justcamh, it casts you as a hapless gnome who is trapped inside a colossal living edifice. Aside from running and jumping, you have the power to copy-paste, move, rotate or delete chunks of the very scenery.

At its simplest, this might involve lifting a wall out of the way, or cropping pieces of hanging stone to create a staircase. But there are also hidden spells you can activate by arranging the tiles into certain patterns, in addition to more familiar props such as pistons that shove other blocks around.

There are nine "worlds" within the Nonolith, arranged on a 3X3 grid, and they can be completed many ways. The overall goal is to escape, but if all you do is escape, the Steam page will be deeply disappointed in you. "For the most adventurous, escape is only the beginning," it thrills. "Reach the highest level of mastery and the Nonolith will succumb to your will. Power awaits the few who dare to wield ultimate control."
There's a Nonolith demo on Steam, with the full game coming later this year. I get a slight Animal Well and/or Fez vibe from the thing, though both of those trade in dastardly unlockables.

articles.headline: Game, set and tache: Carlos Alcaraz joins growing trend for a stylish top lip
keyFacts: Tennis player Carlos Alcaraz debuted a new moustache at the Shanghai Masters after he and his team agreed to grow them if he won the Japan Open.
Barbers and cultural scholars report that thin moustaches are making a significant comeback among young men and male celebrities.
Scholars suggest the trend allows young men to signal maturity, curate a specific form of manliness, and distance themselves from heavy beards.
body: The tennis superstar Carlos Alcaraz might have been knocked out of the Shanghai Masters in straight sets earlier this week, but he did so sporting a moustache that became almost as remarked upon as his aptitude for a sneaky drop shot.

“I always wanted to step on the court at least once with the moustache,” Alcaraz said. The Spaniard and his team had all agreed to take the facial-hair plunge if he won the Japan Open, which he did for a second straight year. “¡Bigotes para todos!” or “moustaches for everyone”, they apparently cheered at the end of the match.
At Milan fashion week last month, the Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi sported a thin strip of hair on his top lip as he watched his girlfriend, Kendall Jenner, model for the Bottega Veneta show.

A moustachioed Harry Styles is roughly halfway through his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York. The actor Timothée Chalamet, who kept his Marty Supreme ’tache on throughout awards season, has been playing around with his facial hair again, adding a goatee.
On TikTok, gen Z men with moustaches are plentiful, as are tutorials for how to grow and style them – alongside almost as many videos from older generations questioning them.

High street barber shops are seeing evidence of it, too. At Citadel in Sheffield, more young men are asking for moustaches, and a large number are asking specifically for thin ones, which the owner, Marie Williams, describes as “[a] low maintenance, easygoing moustache that’s attainable to most”.
According to Jay Byrne, a barber at Dog House barbers in Birmingham and a former British barber of the year: “The moustache is certainly making a comeback, particularly among younger men.”
The moustaches appearing on young men’s faces are a long way from the bushier ones seen in the 1970s and 80s, epitomised by Tom Selleck in Magnum PI.

They seem more to hark back to the Hollywood stars of the 40s and 50s such as David Niven and Clark Gable. “We’re seeing a move away from the heavier, traditional moustaches … towards a much more refined, deliberately styled look,” says Byrne.

“Achieving the look is all about precision, proportion and understanding what suits the individual’s facial structure. It’s not simply a case of growing a moustache and leaving it alone. The shape, thickness and detailing are what make the difference.”
According to Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University: “Skinny moustaches are a sign of difference, especially from men who keep beards.”

Given the rise of the manosphere and the complicated state of masculinity at the moment, Morgan thinks these skinnier moustaches could be intended to steer clear of signalling alpha masculinity. “Young men want to demonstrate a carefully curated form of ‘manliness’,” she says.
For these young male celebrities in particular, Morgan thinks it could be “an expression of ageing”.

“Timothée Chamalet is 30, Jacob Elordi is 29 … it could well be a sign that they want to show that they are mature, they have entered a new phase of life, and want to be seen as more ‘manly’ while remaining youthful.”

For 34-year-old Ncuti Gatwa, who starred in the most recent series of Doctor Who, it has certainly been a way to lean into his age after making his name while playing a schoolboy in the hit TV drama Sex Education.
Gatwa told the Radio Times: “I’d spent the last four years playing a child [in Sex Education], at the age of 30, so I said: ‘Let me have my moustache back.’”

The fashion historian Tony Glenville once had a curly moustache but, he says, “like many men, [I] got rid of facial hair during the mask-wearing times of Covid”. He says it is a trend “among young men who’ve not really seen it around so much recently”. Facial hair, as with all things, “has huge fashion phases for men”.

Movember, which launched in 2003 and has grown into a global movement, sees men grow moustaches for the month of November to raise money for charity and has arguably made facial hair more popular again.
For such a small slither of hair, the moustache is historically and culturally freighted. It can symbolise freedom and has long held a central position in gay culture.

While the moustache might be a “trend” in western culture, in other cultures it is much more of a constant. From romance to war, religion to masculinity and sexuality, moustaches connote different things in different contexts.
Luckily for anyone wanting to give a thin moustache a whirl, according to barber Williams, it is a style that “requires minimal upkeep; just a few snips with the scissors to maintain”.

articles.headline: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
keyFacts: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives and injured several people, including an American photojournalist, in the West Bank.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten and hospitalized while reporting on the olive harvest, the newspaper said.
Israeli police stated they would investigate reports of the injured foreign journalist and bring those involved to justice.
body: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.
The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital and posted online."We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground," she said, "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also stole her cameras and phone.

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement the paper was relieved that Levine received medical care and is safe, but denounced the violence against her.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.
The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to harvest their olives. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.
Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports and contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the State Department said, without mentioning the assault of the American photojournalist.
There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The United Nations' humanitarian office for Gaza and the West Bank said settler attacks during the olive harvest season have killed one Palestinian and damaged more than 2,500 olive trees or saplings.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another assault earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah, who handles the Middle East for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said.
She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities fail to do anything to stop the violence.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and a violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.
